pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11. Palaeoart and speculation — how artists reconstruct extinct animals, and how to tell what is KNOWN from bones vs what is an informed GUESS — taught by separating evidence from inference and calibrating confidence.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y6 Evolution & inheritance and KS2 working-scientifically (distinguishing evidence from opinion; interpreting data).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence) plus the nature-of-science understanding that claims are based on evidence and can be revised; inferences beyond the evidence are provisional.
• Operational details: bones give reliable data — size, posture, muscle attachments, sometimes feather impressions or melanosomes (colour clues). Skin colour, patterning, soft tissue, sounds and behaviour are usually GUESSED from living relatives (birds, crocodiles) and function. Track how reconstructions CHANGED (scaly tail-draggers vs feathered active animals; feathered vs scaly Velociraptor) as evidence improved.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): sort features of a dinosaur picture into 'we know this from bones' vs 'the artist guessed'. Tier B (transitional, ~10): justify a guess using a living relative. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain why palaeoart changes over time and why two accurate artists can still draw the same dinosaur differently.
bestPractices: Explicitly separate evidence (from bones) from inference (from living relatives/function) and label the confidence of each claim.
Use the history of reconstructions to show knowledge is provisional — changing art reflects better evidence, not past 'mistakes'.
Justify speculation by analogy to living relatives (phylogenetic bracketing with birds and crocodiles), modelling disciplined inference.
Celebrate that multiple defensible reconstructions can coexist where evidence is silent — uncertainty is honest, not failure.
Highlight rare evidence that shifts a guess to knowledge (preserved feathers, melanosome colour) so children see how the boundary moves.
keyRepresentations: A layered reconstruction: skeleton → muscle → skin → colour, each tagged by confidence.
A green/amber/red 'known / inferred / guessed' confidence overlay on a dinosaur image.
Side-by-side 'then vs now' reconstructions of the same species.
A living-relative reference panel (bird, crocodile) used to justify inferences.
A feather/melanosome fossil that upgrades a guess to evidence.
commonMisconceptions: 'Dinosaur pictures show exactly what they looked like' — colour, patterning and much soft tissue are informed guesses.
'Old reconstructions were just wrong' — they reflected the evidence then; science updated as more was found.
'We can never know anything for sure, so any guess is as good as another' — inferences are constrained by evidence and living relatives, not free invention.
'Feathers on dinosaurs are artistic fantasy' — many are supported by fossil feather impressions.
'If artists disagree, the science is broken' — legitimate uncertainty allows multiple evidence-consistent depictions.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: palaeoart and the evidence/inference boundary. Learners distinguish what fossils reliably tell us (size, the basic posture the bones allow, muscle-attachment scars, and for some species preserved feather impressions, quill knobs or pigment-structure colour clues) from what is informed speculation (skin colour, patterning, most soft tissue, sounds, behaviour) inferred from living relatives such as birds and crocodiles. They calibrate confidence on each claim and see how reconstructions change — e.g. a scaly Velociraptor becoming a feathered, alert, bird-like animal — as evidence improves, understanding this as science updating rather than past 'mistakes'.

activities.title: Reconstruction studio: build a dinosaur, rate your confidence
feedback: If a learner marks colour as 'known', prompt: colour rarely fossilises — unless a pigment-structure (melanosome) study exists, colour is speculative; re-rate it red or amber.

If a learner rates the skeleton's size or basic stance as a guess, point out these are strongly constrained by the bones and are high-confidence, even though finer details such as tail angle have been reinterpreted over time.
Praise justifications that cite a specific living relative or a preserved fossil feature, since that is disciplined inference rather than free invention.
activities.rationale: Actively constructing and justifying each choice, rather than only labelling a finished image, is intended to exercise the evidence-versus-inference judgement live and tie each confidence rating to a reason.
sourceClaims: Palaeoartists reconstruct extinct animals by combining hard evidence from bones (size, posture, muscle attachments, sometimes preserved feathers or pigment structures) with informed inference from living relatives for features like soft tissue, colour and behaviour.
learnerActions: Start from a verified, locked skeleton and note which features the bones directly give or strongly constrain: overall size, basic stance, and muscle-anchoring scars.
Add layers in order — muscle (inferred from attachment scars), then skin and feathers where relevant, then colour and patterning.
For each choice, mark a confidence level: green ('known from bones'), amber ('inferred from living relatives or function'), red ('a guess — nothing like this is preserved').
Write a one-line justification for each amber/red choice, e.g. 'birds and crocodiles have patterned skin, so I inferred patterning' or 'no pigment is preserved here, so the colour is my guess'.
Compare your finished reconstruction with a classmate's and identify where you both had to guess versus where the evidence pinned things down.
activities.intendedInsight: Building a reconstruction layer by layer makes the boundary between evidence and inference tangible: the deeper, structural layers are well-constrained by bones, while surface colour and patterning are usually informed guesses.

activities.title: Then vs now: the same bones, a different picture
feedback: If a learner calls the old version simply 'wrong', reframe: it reflected the evidence available at the time; new finds (feathered theropods, feather impressions) shifted the picture.
Reinforce that the skeleton barely changed while the interpretation of posture and the surface did — showing which parts are stable evidence and which are revisable inference.
activities.rationale: Using the history of reconstructions concretely models the nature of science: claims are evidence-based and provisional, and inferences beyond the evidence can be revised.
sourceClaims: Dinosaur reconstructions have changed markedly over time — e.g. from scaly, sluggish, tail-dragging depictions to active, often feathered, tail-elevated animals — as fossil evidence (including feathered theropods and melanosome colour studies) accumulated.
learnerActions: Examine two reconstructions of the same species made at different times — for example an older scaly Velociraptor and a modern feathered, active, more bird-like one.
Note the broader trend in older dinosaur art toward sluggish, tail-dragging poses and in modern art toward active, tail-elevated animals, without assuming every descriptor fits every species.
List what stayed the same (the underlying skeleton and proportions) and what changed (posture interpretation, feathers, activity level).
Explain what kind of discovery could cause such a change — e.g. finding feathered theropod fossils or feather impressions, or a melanosome colour study.
Argue whether the older picture was 'wrong' or was the best guess given the evidence available then.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing palaeoart reflects better evidence, not failure; science revises its best-supported picture as new fossils are found.

activities.title: Interview the palaeoartist
feedback: If a learner treats the artist's colour choice as fact, have them ask the follow-up: 'What fossil evidence supports that exact colour?' — usually none, so it is a defensible guess, not knowledge.
Encourage learners to notice when the artist cites birds or crocodiles, which is phylogenetic bracketing used to constrain a guess.
activities.rationale: Hearing an expert articulate their reasoning can model disciplined inference and its limits, complementing the hands-on build; this is a proposed companion, not a verified-superior medium.
sourceClaims: Palaeoartists reconstruct extinct animals by combining hard evidence from bones (size, posture, muscle attachments, sometimes preserved feathers or pigment structures) with informed inference from living relatives for features like soft tissue, colour and behaviour.
learnerActions: Role-play or discuss with a 'palaeoartist' the questions: 'Which parts of your painting could you defend to a scientist, and which are your best guess?' and 'Why did you add feathers?' and 'How did you decide the colour?'
Capture the artist's answers as a two-column list: defensible-from-evidence versus best-guess.
Identify at least one feature the artist would upgrade from guess to evidence if a particular fossil were found (e.g. a feather impression or preserved pigment structures).
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoned speculation is justified by analogy to living relatives and function, and the line between known and guessed can move when rare evidence (preserved feathers, pigment structures) appears.

activities.title: Sort the features: evidence or guess?
feedback: If a learner sorts feathers as 'guess/fashion', check the species: where feather impressions or quill knobs have been found for it or its close relatives, feathers are evidenced, not artistic fantasy; where they have not, they remain an informed inference rather than a certainty.
If a learner sorts colour as 'known', remind them colour rarely fossilises unless pigment structures are preserved.
activities.rationale: A sorting task can sharpen the evidence/inference distinction as a check on classification; it checks the judgement rather than eliciting learners' own construction, so pair it with the build activity.
sourceClaims: Palaeoartists reconstruct extinct animals by combining hard evidence from bones (size, posture, muscle attachments, sometimes preserved feathers or pigment structures) with informed inference from living relatives for features like soft tissue, colour and behaviour.
learnerActions: Given a list of features of a dinosaur picture — size, posture, colour, patterning, feathers, call/sound — sort each into 'known from fossils' or 'informed guess'.
For the feathers entry, decide using whether direct fossil evidence of feathers (feather impressions or quill knobs on the bones) has been found for that species or group, not personal taste.
Explain in a sentence why colour and sound usually fall under 'guess' while size and basic posture fall under 'known' (because the bones strongly constrain them).
Answer: why is a feathered Velociraptor now favoured over a scaly one?
activities.intendedInsight: The same reconstruction mixes well-evidenced features with speculative ones, and feathers can be an evidenced feature (from fossil impressions), not mere decoration.

constraints: Sorting and labelling tasks check the evidence/inference distinction but do not require learners to construct and justify their own choices; pair them with the build activity so learners exercise the judgement, not just recognise it.

Tapping fixed 'evidence vs guess' labels on a single finished image communicates the idea but does not let learners test alternative reconstructions or feel confidence change as choices change; treat it as a scaffold toward active construction.

A confidence overlay (green/amber/red) is a teaching aid: the specific colour bands are a simplification of a continuous uncertainty and depend on whether evidence like feather impressions or pigment-structure studies exists for that species.

Which features count as 'evidenced' depends on the specific fossils found for a group — do not state blanket rules like 'all colour is unknowable' (pigment structures sometimes preserve) or 'feathers are always evidenced' (it varies by taxon).
Avoid teaching the over-correction that reconstructions are pure invention; the skeleton, proportions and any preserved soft tissue genuinely constrain the picture.
A sculpted 3D model draped over a skeleton is an optional alternative experience; the evidence/inference reasoning is not inherently spatial and reads clearly in 2D — neither medium is required.

Use specific depiction dates and species-specific posture descriptors only when they can be verified for the named species; refer to 'older vs modern' reconstructions where a precise date or detail is unconfirmed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support the general practice of combining bone evidence with inference and the historical change in reconstructions; they do not establish the comparative effectiveness of any specific activity or medium (studio build vs sort vs interview).

The original phrasing that recomputing a confidence meter is 'exactly what teaches' the boundary is a design assertion, not a verified finding; retained as a proposed mechanism, not an established law.

The original row's recommendation gives a '1905' date for the early scaly, tail-dragging Velociraptor depiction. This is anachronistic — Velociraptor was named in 1924, and the cited AMNH claim gives no date — so the specific date was removed from learner-facing activities; a fresh re-audit confirms the date no longer appears in any learner-facing text and it should be re-checked against source materials before any use.

The source's 'sluggish, tail-dragging' and 'tail-elevated' descriptors characterise older large-dinosaur art in general; applying them specifically to Velociraptor (a small dromaeosaur) is imprecise, so they are now framed as a broad historical trend while the scaly→feathered change is kept specific to Velociraptor. Exact details should be checked against the source museum materials before classroom use.

Specific examples (older scaly Velociraptor vs modern feathered depiction, melanosome colour studies) are illustrative of the broader claim about changing reconstructions; exact details should be verified against source museum materials before classroom use.

probeDeeper: Our picture of Velociraptor changed from scaly to feathered. What kind of discovery would cause a change like that?
Two artists draw the same dinosaur in different colours — is one of them wrong? How would we ever know?
Which is better evidenced: the shape of its skull or the colour of its skin? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The skeleton, size, and — now — that it had feathers are known from fossils, because feather traces and skin impressions have been found. But the exact colour and patterning are mostly informed speculation, since colour rarely fossilises. Palaeoart is evidence PLUS reasoned guessing, and it changes as new fossils turn up.

errorPatterns.pattern: The picture shows exactly what the dinosaur looked like, colour and all.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort features into evidenced (bones, size, feather traces) versus speculative (colour, patterning); colour rarely fossilises.
errorPatterns.distractor: Scientists know its exact colours and patterns from the fossils.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats every detail, including colour, as directly known from fossils.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's all just made up by artists — fossils tell us nothing about how they looked.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show how the skeleton, proportions and feather impressions genuinely constrain the picture; it's evidence plus reasoning, not free invention.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's all just made up; fossils tell us nothing about appearance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses the whole reconstruction as invention, over-correcting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Feathers on dinosaurs are only an artist's fashion, not real evidence.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to preserved feather fossils on theropods; the feathers are an evidenced feature, not decoration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the feathers were added for looks, not based on fossils.

responseLevels.gap: Treats palaeoart as exact photographic truth, or dismisses it all as pure invention.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes fossil-evidenced features from informed speculation, explains colour rarely fossilises, and recognises reconstructions update with new finds (the feathered Velociraptor case).
responseLevels.partial: Says 'some of it is guessed' but can't sort which features are evidenced (skeleton, feathers) from which are speculative (colour).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A museum shows a brightly coloured, feathered Velociraptor. How much of that picture do scientists actually KNOW from fossils, and how much is informed guessing? Explain which parts are which.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the picture is exact truth says scientists know it all, colour included. A child who understands separates the evidenced parts (skeleton, feathers) from the speculative parts (colour), and knows the picture updates with evidence.
